lesson.title: The Spark of Novelty: How Mutation Fuels Evolution
lesson.summary: Mutation is the ultimate source of all new genetic variation in a population, and although it changes allele frequencies only very slowly on its own, without it natural selection and every other evolutionary force would eventually run out of raw material to act on.
lesson.body:
Every other mechanism discussed in this unit, drift, gene flow, and the different forms of natural selection, works by reshuffling or filtering genetic variation that already exists in a population. Mutation is different: it is the process that creates new variation in the first place. Recall from point mutations that a single change in a DNA sequence, a substitution, insertion, or deletion of one or a few bases, can alter a gene's product or its regulation. When such a change occurs in a cell line that produces gametes, it can be passed on to offspring and become a heritable allele that did not exist in the population before. This is also the first of the five Hardy-Weinberg assumptions to consider. A population in equilibrium is explicitly assumed to have no new mutations entering its gene pool, and any population that does experience mutation has, by definition, the potential to evolve.

It is important to be precise about mutation's actual role, because it is easy to overstate. Mutation rates at any single gene are typically very low, and any individual new mutation is far more likely to be neutral, having no meaningful effect on the organism, or mildly harmful, than it is to be beneficial. A mutation is also random with respect to an organism's needs. DNA replication errors and mutagen exposure do not preferentially produce whatever change would happen to help the organism survive its current environment. On its own, mutation is much too slow and too undirected a process to reshape a population's allele frequencies dramatically within a human observer's lifetime, which is why, for very short term studies, some populations can look approximately mutation free without the assumption being seriously wrong.

A well documented human example shows how mutation and natural selection work together over longer timescales. In most mammals, including most humans, the ability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, declines after weaning as production of the enzyme lactase shuts down. At some point in human history, a mutation arose that kept the lactase gene switched on into adulthood. In populations with a long history of dairy farming, particularly in parts of Northern Europe and among some pastoralist populations in Africa and the Middle East, that mutation rose to high frequency because individuals who carried it could digest milk as a reliable food source throughout life, a real reproductive and survival advantage in those specific cultural and environmental contexts tied to population genetics. In populations without that same dairying history, the ancestral, lactase declining version of the gene remained far more common. The mutation itself was a single, chance event. What population genetics and natural selection did afterward, in each population's particular circumstances, is a separate story.

This example captures mutation's real importance: every heritable trait that natural selection has ever acted on, every allele that a population's fitness differences depend on, ultimately traces back to some mutation that happened first. Selection cannot invent a new allele. It can only act on variation that mutation, sometimes many generations earlier, already supplied. This is why, even though a single mutation rarely shifts allele frequencies on its own, the two processes together, mutation continuously generating new variation and selection continuously filtering it, are what make long term adaptation possible at all. A population that could somehow eliminate mutation entirely would not stay perfectly adapted forever. It would gradually lose its ability to respond to new challenges, because it would have no new variation left to select from.
